trial_name: Hayes — Supranormal Oxygen Delivery in Critical Illness (1994)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Hayes MA, Timmins AC, Yau EHS, Palazzo M, Hinds CJ, Watson D. Elevation of systemic oxygen delivery in the treatment of critically ill patients. N Engl J Med. 1994;330(24):1717-1722.
one_liner: In high-risk ICU patients, dobutamine-driven supranormal oxygen delivery targets increased CI and DO2 but not VO2, and was associated with higher mortality (ICU 50% vs 30%, P=0.04).

pico.population: High-risk critically ill adults (sepsis, ARDS, major surgery) with failure to achieve supranormal targets (CI >4.5 L/min/m², DO2 >600 mL/min/m², VO2 >170 mL/min/m²) after fluid resuscitation.
pico.intervention: Supranormal-target dobutamine strategy: dobutamine 5–200 mcg/kg/min titrated to achieve CI >4.5, DO2 >600, VO2 >170 simultaneously, plus dopamine 2 mcg/kg/min, volume optimisation to plateau of LVSWI vs PAOP, norepinephrine to maintain MAP 80 mmHg.
pico.comparison: Standard care: dobutamine only if CI <2.8 L/min/m²; otherwise identical haemodynamic support (dopamine, fluids, norepinephrine).

related_trials: Gattinoni et al. 1995 (NEJM goal-directed hemodynamic therapy)

background.existing_knowledge: The ‘supranormal oxygen delivery’ concept arose from observational and interventional perioperative work suggesting that survivors of major stress states achieve higher CI and DO2 than non-survivors, and that protocolised targeting of these values (often using pulmonary artery catheters and inotropes) could reduce complications and mortality in selected high‑risk surgical cohorts.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether this strategy applies to heterogeneous high-risk ICU patients with established organ failure.
background.hypothesis: In a heterogeneous, high‑risk ICU population (including sepsis syndrome/shock, ARDS, and high‑risk surgical/medical admissions) who fail to reach predefined supranormal targets with volume expansion alone, does dobutamine‑driven augmentation of CI/DO2/VO2 improve clinical outcomes versus standard haemodynamic support?

methods.design: Prospective, randomised, controlled, two-centre ICU trial (open-label).
methods.setting: ICUs at two hospitals; consecutive high-risk admissions screened over two years.

inclusion: High-risk surgical patients (criteria from Shoemaker et al.)
Non-surgical patients with life-threatening cardiorespiratory illness (acute respiratory failure or septic shock)
After initial fluid resuscitation, failure to reach all three targets (CI >4.5 L/min/m², DO2 >600 mL/min/m², VO2 >170 mL/min/m²)

methods.intervention: Supranormal-target dobutamine strategy: dobutamine 5–200 mcg/kg/min titrated to achieve CI >4.5 L/min/m², DO2 >600 mL/min/m², and VO2 >170 mL/min/m² simultaneously. All patients received dopamine 2 mcg/kg/min, volume optimisation to plateau of left ventricular stroke-work index vs PAOP, and norepinephrine (0.05–20 mcg/kg/min) if needed to maintain MAP 80 mmHg. Safety limits: hold for sinus tachycardia >130 bpm, tachyarrhythmia, or ECG ischaemia.
methods.comparison: Standard support: dobutamine only if CI <2.8 L/min/m². Otherwise identical platform (dopamine, fluids, norepinephrine).
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 130 per group (80% power to detect 15% absolute mortality reduction from 33% to 18%); trial stopped early after 100 patients randomised (50 per group) due to interim analysis showing harm.
secondary_outcomes: Physiological variables (CI, DO2, VO2, O2 extraction ratio, MAP) incremental AUC

headline_bullets: Stopped early after interim analysis; ICU mortality 50% vs 30% (P=0.04), hospital mortality 54% vs 34% (P=0.04).
Dobutamine increased CI (P<0.001) and DO2 (P=0.0012) but not VO2 (P=0.12) or lactate (P=0.2 at 48h).
35/50 treatment patients failed to achieve all three targets simultaneously; 24/50 had dose-limiting complications (tachycardia, ischaemia, hypertension, arrhythmias).
Nine patients who achieved targets with volume alone (not randomised) all survived.

outcomes_table.note: Excess deaths largely attributed to multiple organ failure
Median predicted risk of death (APACHE II-based): 34% in both groups
Other causes: intractable hypotension 4 vs 4; cardiac event 4 vs 2
50/50 vs 21/50 received dobutamine; 17/50 treatment patients received ≥50 mcg/kg/min
Baseline lactate similar (2.2 vs 2.1, P=0.69); both groups decreased over 48h
Treatment group CI AUC significantly higher
Treatment group had lower O2 extraction
Tachycardia >130 bpm (12), ECG ischaemia (8), hypertension (5), tachyarrhythmias (2)

safety: Tachycardia >130 bpm: 12 patients in treatment group
ECG evidence of myocardial ischaemia: 8 patients
No other adverse events reported; control group complications not detailed.
Higher norepinephrine maximal dose in treatment group (median 1.2 vs 0.23 mcg/kg/min, P=0.029).

domains.notes: Randomisation used a table of random numbers after fluid resuscitation; allocation concealment not described.
Open-label administration of inotropes/vasopressors; primary outcomes (mortality) are objective, but attribution of cause of death is interpretive.
All 100 randomised patients included in outcome reporting; no post-randomisation exclusions.

In treatment group, 35/50 did not achieve all three targets simultaneously despite dobutamine; dose increments limited by complications in 24/50. Control group: 21/50 received dobutamine (up to 200 mcg/kg/min) if CI <2.8, potentially diluting between-group differences.
Groups similar for age (median 63.5 vs 62), APACHE II (median 18 vs 18), APACHE III (median 58 vs 63), and organ-failure score (median 1 vs 1).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: randomisation and complete follow-up for hard endpoints support internal validity, but open-label delivery, feasibility limits (failure to reach targets in 35/50), and early stopping reduce confidence in the stability of the effect estimate.

domains.notes: High-risk, heterogeneous ICU cohort (sepsis, ARDS, major surgery); exclusion of patients with pre-existing cardiac disease and haematologic cancer may limit applicability to contemporary ICUs with higher cardiac comorbidity.
Management relied on pulmonary artery catheterisation, fixed dopamine infusion, haemoglobin target >10 g/dL, and explicit CI/DO2/VO2 targets—elements that differ from many modern protocols.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is context-limited (two-centre, PA catheter–based era), but the central message—systemic DO2 augmentation may not translate into improved tissue utilisation and may cause harm in established critical illness—remains conceptually relevant.

strengths: Prospective randomised controlled design in a heterogeneous ICU population directly testing a prevalent physiological strategy.
Explicit haemodynamic targets and dosing ranges (dobutamine 5–200 mcg/kg/min; norepinephrine 0.05–20 mcg/kg/min) with prespecified safety limits.
Objective primary outcomes (ICU and hospital mortality) with complete reporting for all randomised patients.
Dense physiological sampling and prespecified 48-hour incremental AUC summaries to quantify exposure and separation.
limitations: Stopped early with only 50 patients per arm (vs planned 130 per arm), limiting precision and increasing susceptibility to random high-magnitude effects.
Unblinded intervention delivery; co-interventions and bedside decision-making could be influenced by allocation.
Feasibility constraints: 35/50 treatment patients could not achieve all three targets simultaneously; dose-limiting tachycardia/ischaemia common.
Era- and technology-specific care (routine pulmonary artery catheterisation, fixed dopamine infusion, haemoglobin target >10 g/dL) may not map cleanly to contemporary practice.

critical_appraisal.summary: While this trial raised important safety concerns about supranormal DO2 targets, its early termination, small sample, and open-label design limit confidence in the magnitude of harm; however, the physiological disconnect (improved DO2 without improved VO2) and higher mortality provide a strong cautionary signal.
weaknesses: Limited target attainment in treatment group

sections.authors_conclusion: In high-risk ICU patients, protocolised dobutamine to achieve supranormal oxygen transport targets increased DO2 without improving VO2 or lactate, and was associated with higher mortality; the findings challenge the routine use of fixed systemic DO2 goals in established critical illness.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Does not support routine use of supranormal DO2 targets in general ICU patients; inotrope use should be selective for cardiac dysfunction with hypoperfusion.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: High-risk critically ill adults with established organ failure, not perioperative pre-emptive optimisation.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not necessarily implicate dobutamine in all settings; perioperative goal-directed therapy in selected surgical patients may have different risk-benefit.
implementation_caveats: Avoid routine dobutamine escalation to fixed supranormal targets in ICU.
Catecholamine-related complications (tachycardia, ischaemia) may limit benefit.
Monitoring and goals may need to be individualised.

controversies.notes: Single-centre perioperative goal-directed haemodynamic trials often showed reduced complications/mortality, whereas multicentre ICU cohorts showed no benefit or harm, raising questions about timing (pre-emptive vs established organ failure) and protocol fidelity.

A multicentre RCT of goal-oriented haemodynamic therapy in critically ill patients similarly failed to show outcome benefit, reinforcing the concern that late systemic DO2 augmentation may not improve clinical outcomes.

A broad meta-analysis of haemodynamic optimisation trials found an overall mortality reduction when combining studies, driven primarily by perioperative/trauma contexts; effects were not uniform across sepsis/organ-failure populations.

Current sepsis/shock guidelines emphasise individualised haemodynamic targets, dynamic fluid responsiveness, serial perfusion assessment, and selective inotrope use—rather than fixed supranormal systemic oxygen transport goals.
Contemporary perioperative consensus has become more cautious about routine goal-directed haemodynamic therapy and fixed inotrope infusions, narrowing indications to selected settings.

context_related_trials.relation: Multicentre RCT of goal-oriented hemodynamic therapy in critically ill patients, also failed to show benefit, supporting the Hayes findings.
Earlier perioperative studies that inspired the concept; showed benefit in high-risk surgical patients, but results not replicated in heterogeneous ICU populations.

unresolved_questions: Can supranormal DO2 targets benefit specific subgroups (e.g., trauma, perioperative) with different timing?
What is the role of microcirculatory/perfusion endpoints as opposed to systemic DO2?
Is there a safe and effective protocol for inotrope escalation in ICU patients with persistent hypoperfusion?

numbers_to_remember: 35/50 treatment patients failed to achieve all three targets simultaneously
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In established ICU critical illness, dobutamine-driven supranormal DO2 targets did not improve VO2 or lactate and were associated with increased mortality, challenging the routine pursuit of fixed systemic oxygen transport goals.
